At ten, Varun stumbled over "population" when he read aloud, and heard a titter. He stuck his tongue out sideways, flapped his arms like a chicken and read on. Everyone laughed, and Farida Ma'am waited with a smile. Varun took his seat with a grin and a racing heart.
At fifteen, Varun lived in a class chat where everything was answered with pictures. After Gargi shared her first slide of a group presentation, he dropped in a GIF of a potato dancing wildly. To him it meant "this is fun, I'm enjoying it". The rest of the group sent laughing faces. Gargi went quiet. Later she messaged him privately: "Was the potato about my slides?" Varun stared at the message. He had not thought how a joke that made sense to his friends might look to someone new. He typed, "No! I meant I was happy. Sorry, it's a silly thing we do 🙂. Your slide was good." Gargi replied, "Okay. I wondered." The next day, he added a line of plain words to his next reply.

qa.q: What did Varun send after Gargi shared her first slide?
qa.a: He sent a GIF of a potato dancing wildly.

qa.q: How is Varun's humour at ten like his GIF at fifteen, and where does it go wrong?
qa.a: Both are quick ways to bring a light mood: a chicken flap at ten and a dancing potato at fifteen. The GIF made sense to his friends but Gargi, as an outsider, could read it as mocking her slide, so an in-joke may confuse or hurt someone who does not share it.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when she went quiet and then asked if the potato was about her slides?
qa.a: She felt unsure and a little hurt, wondering whether the joke was aimed at her work.

qa.q: What could Varun do to keep the chat friendly to newcomers?
qa.a: He can add a few plain words to a joke, explain the in-joke to new members, and check when someone seems left out.

grounding: A class clown's joke to cover embarrassment (3891) and the same boy's meme humour as shared language that can confuse an outsider (2595).

At five, Sahil stopped at the door of a wedding hall and hid behind Papa Arnab's legs. Aunties bent down to greet him, and he pressed his face into Papa's trousers. Papa did not pull him out. He stayed close, one hand on Sahil's head, until the noise felt bearable.
At fifteen, Sahil sat in the last row of the classroom, looking at the back of Anirban's head. For months he rehearsed the sentence he would say at the school gate. He practised it in the shower and on the bus, changing a word here and there. Every time the moment came, he told himself, "Not today." Staying silent felt like relief, each time. Then in April he saw Anirban laughing with another classmate at the canteen, walking home with them, sharing earphones. Sahil looked away. That night Papa Arnab found him sitting on the stairs. "You look heavy. Want to walk?" On the street, Sahil said, "I never said anything, and now it's too late." Papa nodded. "It hurts. If you ever want to try again, with anyone, I can sit with you while you plan a small first sentence," he said.

qa.q: Where did Sahil hide when he was five?
qa.a: He hid behind Papa Arnab's legs at the door of a wedding hall.

qa.q: How is Sahil's silence about Anirban like his hiding at the wedding, and what did the silence cost him?
qa.a: Both times Sahil stayed away from what scared him, and it gave a moment of relief. At the wedding, Papa's nearness helped him cope, but at fifteen months of not speaking meant Anirban began talking with someone else, and he lost any chance of a yes.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when he said, "I never said anything, and now it's too late"?
qa.a: He felt regret and sadness, hurt by the missed chance and by his own silence.

qa.q: What could Sahil try next time he is drawn to someone?
qa.a: He can plan one small, respectful first sentence, with Papa's or a friend's support, and accept that a no is possible.

grounding: A child hiding to avoid a scary thing (3921) and a teen who never speaks to his crush and loses the chance, showing the cost of avoidance (6323).

When baby Indu came home, five-year-old Alka, who had spoken in full sentences for years, began to say "wa-wa" for water and hold her arms up to be carried. She followed Mummy Parul from room to room and sucked her thumb at night. Mummy noticed and did not scold. She sat Alka on her lap while she fed the baby. "There is still room on my lap for you," she said, and Alka leaned against her, quiet.
A month later, Alka woke up hot and sniffly. She lay in bed and asked in a small voice, "Bottle, Mummy?" Mummy Parul, who had put the bottle away a long time ago, brought it warm with milk and did not comment. Alka also asked to sleep in Mummy's bed and spoke in a soft baby voice. Mummy tucked her in with her arm and said, "You're not feeling well. I'm here." She told Papa that if the illness kept going or worried her, she would ring the doctor. Two days later, Alka was chattering in her usual voice and asked for her own bed.

qa.q: What word did Alka use for water after the baby came?
qa.a: She said "wa-wa".

qa.q: How do Alka's baby talk after the baby and during her illness compare, and what did Mummy Parul do in both?
qa.a: In both, Alka went back to babyish ways, first to ask if there was still room for her and later because she felt unwell. Mummy Parul never scolded; she made room on her lap and brought the bottle, and Alka went back to her usual voice.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling when she began to say "wa-wa" and asked to be carried?
qa.a: She felt unsure of her place and wanted to be looked after, worried that the new baby had taken her spot.

qa.q: What could Mummy Parul do if Alka's baby talk goes on for a long time after she recovers?
qa.a: She can keep giving warm attention and special time, praise Alka's big-girl moments without shaming her, and check with the doctor if it worries her.

grounding: A child regresses to baby talk after a sibling arrives (3881) and again when ill (4154), and a parent answers without shame.

At nine, Chinmay put his drawing on the table for Papa Samir. Papa looked at the maths sheet beside it and said, "Ninety. Ten marks gone. Do it again." He did not mention the drawing. Chinmay stopped showing his drawings and began to hide any sheet with mistakes.
At twenty, Chinmay was the strongest writer in his college class. Yet when Salma Ma'am mentioned a chance to join the campus magazine, he said no. When a professor suggested a summer fellowship, he said, "Maybe next year." His drafts stayed in a folder, never sent. Salma Ma'am noticed how much ability was going unused. One afternoon she showed him a crumpled first draft of her own, full of arrows and crossed lines. "This is what my article looked like. Nobody sees this part." Then she said, "I saw how much you improved your last essay. Send me the messy version, and I'll tell you what is working." Chinmay stared at the crossed lines. He opened the folder and picked the earliest draft, and his hands were not quite steady.

qa.q: What did Papa Samir say when he saw the maths sheet?
qa.a: He said, "Ninety. Ten marks gone. Do it again."

qa.q: How is Chinmay's behaviour at twenty connected to how Papa Samir reacted when he was nine?
qa.a: Papa looked only at the marks and ignored the drawing, so Chinmay learned to hide anything that was not perfect. At twenty he turned down the magazine and the fellowship and kept his drafts hidden, while Salma Ma'am's praise of his improvement and her own crossed-out draft began to loosen that grip.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling as he opened the folder with unsteady hands?
qa.a: He felt nervous and exposed, afraid that his rough draft would be judged, but also a little hopeful.

qa.q: What could Salma Ma'am do next to keep helping Chinmay?
qa.a: She can keep praising his effort and progress, share more of her own rough drafts, and encourage small steps like sending one piece to the magazine.

grounding: A child answered only on marks (4097) becomes a strong young writer who turns down chances until a teacher praises effort and shows her flawed drafts (3200).

At nine, Tanvir played marbles with Binita outside the tea shop. He won a blue one and gave a small cheer. Five minutes later he lost his favourite red marble, and he sat down on the kerb and cried until his nose ran. Binita offered him two green ones, but he kept looking at the empty spot in his pocket. The loss felt much bigger than the win.
At twenty, Tanvir woke to rising water in the street below his rented room. Volunteers had said residents must go to the community hall and stay there until told it was safe. Tanvir left with his flatmate Noor, but on the way his mind kept returning to the laptop with his project files and his certificates in the drawer. "I'll only run back for ten minutes," he said, turning towards the lane. Noor caught his sleeve. "The water's still rising. We can't." Tanvir pulled away, and a volunteer at the corner in a bright vest stepped in front of him. "Please stay back, brother. Things can be replaced." Tanvir stood at the edge with his fists clenched, then let Noor lead him to the hall, where they waited together until the officials announced the lane was safe.

qa.q: What colour was the marble Tanvir lost at nine?
qa.a: It was his favourite red marble.

qa.q: How do Tanvir's tears over the marble and his urge to return to the flat show the same pull?
qa.a: Losing something he owned hurt him far more than winning felt good at nine. At twenty, worry about his laptop and certificates almost drew him back into rising water, and only Noor and the volunteer's protective steps kept him safe until officials said the lane was safe.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling as he stood at the edge of the lane with his fists clenched?
qa.a: He was anxious and reluctant to let go of his belongings, torn between fear of losing them and the warnings.

qa.q: What could Tanvir do next time he worries about his belongings during an emergency?
qa.a: He can follow the volunteers' advice, keep copies of key files in a safe place ahead of time, and wait until officials say it is safe.

grounding: A child who cries harder over losing a marble than he cheers for winning one (3608) and, as an adult, nearly returns to a flooded home to save belongings (7039).

passage:
At five, Leela stood at the entrance of a neighbour's housewarming and would not move. She grabbed Mummy Damini's dupatta and hid behind her. Mummy did not push her forward. She rested a hand on Leela's back until Leela peeked out at the lights.
At fifteen, Leela lay awake the night before her maths test and knocked on her parents' door. "Papa, will everything be fine?" Papa Vijay said, "Yes, you've prepared well." She went back to bed for ten minutes, then returned. "But what if I forget the formulas?" "You won't." She left, came back again and asked whether she had studied enough. Each answer eased the worry for a few minutes, and then it crept back. In the morning she asked Mummy Damini the same question over breakfast. Mummy gently said, "I notice you keep asking, and the answer helps only for a short while. Shall we talk about how you can calm yourself, and maybe about what the school counsellor could show you?" Leela let out a long breath and nodded.

qa.q: What did Leela grab at the housewarming when she was five?
qa.a: She grabbed Mummy Damini's dupatta and hid behind her.

qa.q: How do Leela's clinging at five and her repeated questions at fifteen show a similar pattern?
qa.a: Both are ways of getting relief from fear by leaning on a parent. At five, Mummy's hand on her back was enough, but at fifteen the reassurance from Papa Vijay eased the worry only for minutes, so Mummy Damini suggested learning to calm herself, with a counsellor.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when she kept coming back to her parents' door?
qa.a: She felt anxious and unsure she could cope alone, and each answer calmed her only briefly.

qa.q: How could Mummy Damini and Papa Vijay respond to Leela's repeated questions?
qa.a: They can stay warm and kind while gently limiting the repeats, help her practise calming herself, and involve the school counsellor.

grounding: A child hides behind a parent (3921) and, as a teen, keeps asking her parents whether everything will be fine, which soothes only briefly (3289).
